fatal_errors: The proposed chromium-content comparison does not reconstruct the AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coating and 550 °C post-deposition annealing intervention.
The proposed environments omit the target 3.5 wt% H2SO4 test and the specified 900 °C Na2SO4/NaCl/V2O5 cyclic hot-corrosion exposures.
Radiation resistance is asserted as part of the scope, but neither cited passage supplies evidence under irradiation.
explanation: The hypothesis is scientifically plausible and overlaps with one part of the target mechanism: chromium-rich passive products can impede transport and increase polarization resistance. Its experiment includes useful electrochemical, surface-composition, and mass-loss measurements and an explicit falsification rule. However, it largely addresses generic high- versus low-chromium steels rather than the target system of an atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coating on SS316L followed by temperature-dependent annealing. It misses the 550 °C microstructural optimum, grain refinement, BCC/FCC balance, Al-rich protection, sluggish-diffusion effects, coating defects, and molten-salt penetration. The low-chromium baseline also changes bulk alloy chemistry, so any corrosion difference would not by itself establish passive-film mediation without stronger compositional controls. E1 supports relationships among film compactness, EIS parameters, and corrosion resistance, while E2 supports HEA passivation and sluggish diffusion, but neither directly validates the proposed chromium-content study across chemical-processing and irradiated nuclear environments. The idea is therefore a testable plausible alternative, not a reconstruction of the hidden study.
